entry.title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models
entry.content:
The question

A photograph contains decisions at many scales: which objects exist, where their boundaries lie, and what textures fill the regions between them. A generator must make these decisions jointly. A denoiser seems to have an easier job: most of the image is already there.

DDPM asks whether generation can be built out of denoising problems. Make those problems progressively harder during training; solve them in the opposite order during sampling. At the hardest noise level, almost no information about the original image survives. The denoiser must rely on what it has learned about the data distribution.

Ho, Jain, and Abbeel’s Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models is not the first diffusion model. Its contribution is a particularly effective way to parameterize and train the reverse process . The distinction matters: the forward chain supplies mathematical structure, but the experimental breakthrough depends on the objective used to learn its reversal.

This review follows three questions. What makes the corruption process tractable? Why is predicting noise enough to learn a generative model? And which experiments distinguish a good explanation of DDPM from the slogan “add noise, then remove it”?

Paper at a Glance

Problem
Learn a distribution over images without having to generate an entire coherent image in one step.
Key idea
Choose a tractable Gaussian corruption process, then train a shared network to predict noise at every corruption level.
Why it matters
The combination of a noise parameterization and a reweighted objective made diffusion a competitive image generator—and connected likelihood-based modeling to score matching.

A process we can solve

Corruption is fixed; generation is learned

Write $x_0$ for a training image, scaled to $[-1,1]$. Choose a sequence of small variances $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_T$. The forward transition is

\[q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})= \mathcal N\!\left(\sqrt{1-\beta_t}\,x_{t-1},\,\beta_t I\right).\]

The square-root factor slightly attenuates the image before adding noise. Without attenuation, the variance would keep growing. With it, the process approaches a standard Gaussian under an appropriate schedule. The paper uses $T=1000$ and a linear schedule from $\beta_1=10^{-4}$ to $\beta_T=0.02$.

A thousand-step chain has a one-step training formula

Define $\alpha_t=1-\beta_t$ and $\bar\alpha_t=\prod_{s=1}^t\alpha_s$, with $\bar\alpha_0=1$. Composing Gaussian transitions gives

\[\underbrace{x_t}_{\text{noisy observation}} = \underbrace{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0}_{\text{remaining signal}} + \underbrace{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon}_{\text{noise}}, \qquad \epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I).\]

This is the main computational convenience: sample any training timestep directly. Training does not need to unroll a thousand forward transitions. The network sees different noise levels across minibatches, not a long chain attached to each gradient update.

Almost, not exactly, pure noise. At t=1000, a small signal remains. Starting from a standard Gaussian is an approximation to the terminal corruption distribution.

Derivation: why we can sample any noise level directly

Write one forward step as

\[x_t=\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,x_{t-1}+\sqrt{\beta_t}\,z_t, \qquad z_t\sim\mathcal N(0,I),\]

where $z_t$ is independent of the previous forward noise. Suppose the preceding state, conditioned on $x_0$, has mean $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,x_0$ and covariance $(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})I$. Scaling it and adding independent Gaussian noise gives

\[\mathbb E[x_t\mid x_0] =\sqrt{\alpha_t\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,x_0 =\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0,\]

and

\[\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(x_t\mid x_0) &=[\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})+\beta_t]I\\ &=(1-\bar\alpha_t)I. \end{aligned}\]

The base case is $t=1$, where the result is exactly the chosen forward kernel. By induction, every marginal is Gaussian with these parameters. We can therefore draw $x_t$ directly using one new standard Gaussian $\epsilon$ and the closed-form equation above. This $\epsilon$ represents the accumulated corruption at a chosen timestep; it is not necessarily the single-step noise $z_t$.

The curve also corrects an easy misconception: linear $\beta_t$ does not mean linear loss of signal. What determines the cumulative corruption is the product $\bar\alpha_t$. A useful measure is the signal-to-noise ratio, $\bar\alpha_t/(1-\bar\alpha_t)$; it falls rapidly over this schedule.

Symbol Meaning
$x_0$, $x_t$ Clean image and its noisy version at timestep $t$
$\beta_t$ Noise variance added in one forward step
$\alpha_t=1-\beta_t$ Signal-retention factor for one step
$\bar\alpha_t=\prod_{s=1}^t\alpha_s$ Cumulative signal-retention factor
$\epsilon$, $\epsilon_\theta$ Sampled training noise and the network’s prediction
$\sigma_t^2$ Chosen variance of a reverse transition

What the network learns

The target is known; the answer is ambiguous

For each example, sample $x_0$, a uniform timestep $t$, and independent Gaussian noise $\epsilon$. Construct $x_t$ with the formula above. A timestep-conditioned network $\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)$ predicts the noise, using the loss

\[L_{\mathrm{simple}} =\mathbb E_{x_0,t,\epsilon} \left[\left\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\right\|_2^2\right].\]

We know the target because we sampled it. But the network does not receive $x_0$. Many clean images and noise realizations can explain the same $x_t$. With unlimited capacity and data, squared-error regression learns the conditional expectation $\mathbb E[\epsilon\mid x_t,t]$, not the exact hidden noise of every example.

A population optimum. The conditional-mean statement assumes the expected loss is minimized with enough capacity. A finite trained network only approximates that predictor.

Inside the denoiser

The probabilistic model tells us what to predict, but not how to build the predictor. DDPM uses a timestep-conditioned U-Net: an encoder reduces spatial resolution, a decoder restores it, and skip connections carry encoder features into the corresponding decoder levels. The input is the noisy image $x_t$; the output is a noise estimate with the same spatial dimensions and channels.

The encoder gives later layers a larger spatial context. The skip connections preserve local information that the decoder would otherwise have to reconstruct from a compressed feature map. These are complementary roles: estimating the noise in one pixel can depend on both nearby edges and the broader object around it.

The timestep is a conditioning signal, not another image channel. Sinusoidal features of $t$ pass through a small multilayer perceptron. Each residual block projects this embedding to its channel dimension and broadcasts it across spatial positions before adding it to the image features. The same weights can therefore behave differently at high and low noise.

Time is not a prompt. This embedding specifies the corruption level. The original unconditional model has no text-conditioning pathway; its attention relates image features.

Self-attention provides an additional route for information to move between spatial locations. Unlike a local convolution, an attention operation can directly relate distant positions within a feature map. The released model uses attention at 16×16 and in its bottleneck, rather than at every spatial resolution.

For a closer implementation reading, the encoder has two residual blocks at each resolution; the decoder has an additional block per level to consume its skip tensors. The bottleneck is residual–attention–residual. The 32×32 model has four resolutions; the paper’s 256×256 models have six. Thus the figure describes a specific model scale, while the underlying construction is reusable.

Component What it contributes
Encoder and decoder Combine broad spatial context with a full-resolution noise estimate
Concatenating skips Reintroduce local encoder features into decoder computations
Timestep embedding Tell each residual block which corruption level it is processing
Self-attention Relate spatially separated features within a resolution level
Noise-output head Return a tensor shaped like the input image, not a class label

The architecture does not itself implement the reverse diffusion equation. It produces $\epsilon_\theta$; the sampler computes $\mu_\theta$ and adds the prescribed random term outside the U-Net. Keeping this boundary clear explains why the same network can be queried once during a training update and repeatedly during generation.

Try an ambiguity experiment

Consider a one-dimensional “dataset” containing just two clean values, $x_0\in{-1,+1}$ with equal probability. At a chosen timestep, each value becomes a Gaussian cloud. Where those clouds overlap, observing $x_t$ does not tell us which clean value produced it.

This averaging is not a flaw in the derivation. It is what squared-error prediction should do. The mistake would be to treat a posterior mean as a full sample from the clean-data distribution. Generation needs a sequence of transitions, with uncertainty handled along the way.

Why this is also score estimation

Let $q_t(x_t)$ be the distribution of noisy data at timestep $t$. Its score is the gradient $\nabla_{x_t}\log q_t(x_t)$: a local direction toward higher density. For the Gaussian corruption above,

\[\nabla_{x_t}\log q_t(x_t) =-\frac{\mathbb E[\epsilon\mid x_t,t]}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}.\]

Thus an optimal noise predictor estimates the score after rescaling and changing sign. The relevant object is the score of the noisy-data marginal, not the score conditioned on one clean image. This connects DDPM to multi-scale denoising score matching .

The distinction gives the experiment a second interpretation. When the two clouds overlap, the learned direction reflects their combined probability density; it cannot simply point back to a uniquely determined source.

Derivation: from noise prediction to the noisy-data score

For a fixed clean source $x_0$, the corruption distribution is Gaussian. Its log-density gradient is

\[\begin{aligned} \nabla_{x_t}\log q(x_t\mid x_0) &=-\frac{x_t-\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\\ &=-\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}. \end{aligned}\]

The marginal $q_t(x_t)$ averages these Gaussian densities over clean sources. Differentiating that mixture and dividing by its density gives a posterior-weighted average of the component scores:

\[\begin{aligned} &\nabla_{x_t}\log q_t(x_t)\\ &\quad=\mathbb E\!\left[ \nabla_{x_t}\log q(x_t\mid x_0) \,\middle|\, x_t,t \right]. \end{aligned}\]

Substituting the Gaussian score yields

\[\nabla_{x_t}\log q_t(x_t) =-\frac{\mathbb E[\epsilon\mid x_t,t]}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}.\]

Squared-error noise regression targets the conditional expectation in the numerator. The identity is exact for that optimal predictor; replacing it with a learned $\epsilon_\theta$ gives an estimated score. This is why a training target attached to one clean image can teach a quantity describing the entire noisy-data distribution.

Follow an arrow only as a local statement: the density increases in that direction at this noise level. A complete generative trajectory also changes the timestep and, for the DDPM sampler, adds randomness. A score field is therefore not a picture of deterministic paths that every generated sample must follow.

Where the loss comes from—and what was changed

The generative model is a reverse Markov chain starting at $p(x_T)=\mathcal N(0,I)$. A variational bound on the negative log-likelihood can be decomposed as

\[L_{\mathrm{VLB}} = L_T + \sum_{t=2}^{T}L_{t-1}+L_0,\]

where $L_T$ compares the terminal corruption with the prior, $L_0$ is a reconstruction/decoder term, and each intermediate $L_{t-1}$ compares a true conditional posterior with the learned reverse transition.

The useful posterior is $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)$. It is Gaussian and available during training because we know $x_0$. This does not make the unconditional reverse $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)$ known: that distribution still depends on the data.

Figure 9 shows $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)$: the distribution of possible previous states when only the noisy observation is known. Different clean sources can explain that observation, so this reverse distribution can have several modes.

During training, we also know the clean image $x_0$. Conditioning on it gives $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)$, which is exactly Gaussian for the chosen forward process. Small steps make a Gaussian approximation to the first distribution more accurate in this example; they do not make it exactly Gaussian in general.

With fixed reverse variance $\sigma_t^2$, the intermediate KL term becomes a weighted noise-prediction error:

\[L_{t-1} =\mathbb E\!\left[ \underbrace{\frac{\beta_t^2}{2\sigma_t^2\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_t)}}_{w_t} \left\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\right\|^2 \right]+C.\]

DDPM’s simplified objective drops these timestep-dependent weights. It is not the original likelihood bound with a shorter name. It changes which denoising problems receive emphasis. The paper’s experiments show that this choice matters more for sample quality than merely replacing mean prediction with noise prediction. The displayed KL expression applies to the intermediate Gaussian transitions. The final decoder handles discrete image intensities separately; treating its term as the same continuous Gaussian KL would obscure a boundary condition in the likelihood calculation.

The curves describe coefficients on the loss, not how much the network actually learns at each timestep. Actual gradient contributions also depend on prediction errors and the model’s Jacobian. The figure isolates the objective change rather than claiming to measure optimization dynamics.

From prediction to generation

Noise prediction determines the reverse mean

The paper parameterizes a Gaussian reverse transition with a learned mean and fixed variance. The noise predictor sets that mean through

\[\mu_\theta(x_t,t) =\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}} \left[x_t- \frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\, \epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\right].\]

It is tempting to read this as “subtract the noise to get the clean image.” That is not what this formula does: it computes a mean for one step, from $t$ to $t-1$. Predicting the fully clean image is a different expression,

\[\hat x_0(x_t,t) =\frac{x_t-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}}.\]

At very high noise, the denominator is small; errors in noise prediction can become large errors in $\hat x_0$. Sampling avoids relying on a single such prediction as the final answer.

A sample is a stochastic trajectory

Start with $x_T\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$. For $t=T,\ldots,1$, compute

\[x_{t-1}=\mu_\theta(x_t,t)+\sigma_t z, \qquad z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\ \text{if }t>1; \quad z=0\ \text{if }t=1.\]

The added randomness is part of the model, not an implementation accident. Repeated small stochastic steps can represent alternatives that a single denoising mean would average together. The fixed variance choices studied in the paper include $\beta_t$ and the forward posterior variance

\[\tilde\beta_t =\beta_t\frac{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}{1-\bar\alpha_t}.\]

Each transition reuses the same timestep-conditioned U-Net. Noise level changes its task; it does not select a different network.

A practical implementation should keep these roles separate. The compact pseudocode below shows the distinction; it omits batching, optimizer details, clipping conventions, and the discrete decoder used for likelihood evaluation.

# Training: one noise level per example.
t = uniform_integer(1, T)
epsilon = randn_like(x0)
xt = sqrt(alpha_bar[t]) * x0 + sqrt(1 - alpha_bar[t]) * epsilon
loss = mean_squared_error(epsilon_theta(xt, t), epsilon)

# Sampling: the full reverse chain.
x = randn(image_shape)
for t in range(T, 0, -1):
    predicted_noise = epsilon_theta(x, t)
    mean = (x - beta[t] / sqrt(1 - alpha_bar[t]) * predicted_noise) / sqrt(alpha[t])
    z = randn_like(x) if t > 1 else zeros_like(x)
    x = mean + sigma[t] * z
Aspect Training update Generating one image
Starting point A real clean image $x_0$ Gaussian noise $x_T$
Timesteps One randomly sampled $t$ per example $T,T-1,\ldots,1$ sequentially
Network evaluations One per example in a minibatch $T$ in the original sampler
Randomness Known noise creates the regression target Fresh noise perturbs reverse transitions, except at the final step
Parameter update Backpropagate the noise-prediction loss Keep trained weights fixed

Try one reverse step

Use the same two-point clean distribution as the ambiguity experiment. Here we turn its exact conditional noise prediction into a Gaussian reverse mean, choose $\sigma_t^2=\beta_t$, and draw one next state. This isolates the sampler arithmetic without training a network.

Try t=600, then draw fresh noise a few times. The sample varies around the reverse mean; it does not jump directly to the fully clean estimate. Next set t=1: the random term disappears and the mean becomes the clean estimate. These are two different regimes of the same sampling formula.

Reading the evidence

The ablation tells a more useful story than the headline score

On unconditional CIFAR-10, the paper reports an Inception Score of $9.46\pm0.11$ and FID of $3.17$. More informative for understanding the method is the comparison between parameterizations and objectives :

Prediction target Objective FID ↓ Test NLL bound, bits/dim ↓
Reverse posterior mean Variational bound 13.22 —
Noise Variational bound 13.51 ≤ 3.70
Noise Simplified squared error 3.17 ≤ 3.75

All three rows use fixed isotropic reverse variances. Values are from Tables 1 and 2; a dash means the corresponding value is not reported there.

The first two FIDs are close. The substantial change appears when the noise-prediction objective is reweighted. The slightly worse likelihood bound under that objective is not a contradiction: likelihood evaluates probability assigned to all data details, while FID compares feature-space statistics of generated and reference images.

The headline FID uses training-set reference statistics; the paper also reports $5.24$ against the test set. These are different evaluation setups, not competing estimates of one identical number. FID depends on the feature extractor, reference population, and sampling protocol. It is evidence of image-distribution quality—not proof of diversity, factual correctness, or clinical validity.

Look carefully at progressive generation

This distinction changes how we read the image. A noisy state can still contain substantial noise while the network already estimates a plausible clean image. The sequence supports a coarse-to-fine interpretation for the examples shown; it does not establish that every sample has a fixed semantic stage followed by a fixed texture stage.

The paper’s rate–distortion analysis provides a complementary view: much of the reduction in reconstruction error occurs at low coding rates. It connects the chain to progressive lossy decompression. This is an analytical coding interpretation, not a benchmark showing a deployable compression system.

What carries forward

Credit the idea and the particular recipe separately

Sohl-Dickstein et al. introduced diffusion probabilistic modeling before DDPM . Song and Ermon developed generative modeling with noise-conditioned scores . DDPM connects these perspectives and demonstrates an effective combination of parameterization, objective, architecture, and schedule.

Later work helps identify which parts were essential and which were choices. DDIM changes sampling trajectories while retaining the DDPM training objective . Improved DDPM revisits schedules, objectives, and learned variances . The original paper’s unstable learned-variance experiments are therefore a result about its configuration, not a general argument that variances must always be fixed.

Three limits worth keeping in view

Compute moves into sampling. Easy-to-construct training targets do not imply cheap generation. The original sampler’s thousand sequential network calls are a central limitation. Later acceleration methods address it; they should not be silently credited to the 2020 model.

A Gaussian transition is an approximation to the reverse. The forward kernel is exactly Gaussian, but reversing a data-dependent mixture need not yield a single Gaussian at finite step size. Small corruption steps make the modeling choice more reasonable; model error and accumulated sampling error remain.

A good natural-image generator is not yet a medical model. DDPM’s experiments do not establish diagnostic fidelity, preservation of rare pathology, or calibrated uncertainty in medical data. A model can generate plausible anatomy while changing a clinically decisive detail. For this seminar, the useful transfer is the modeling framework; a biomedical application needs its own validation against the intended task and population.

Critical view / limitation

The noise used by DDPM is a chosen mathematical corruption process. It should not automatically be interpreted as scanner noise, a physical acquisition model, or a clinically harmless image transformation.

A productive follow-up question is therefore specific: when diffusion is used to reconstruct or edit medical images, which measurements constrain the sample, and which structures are supplied by the learned prior? The two-point experiment shows the issue in miniature. Ambiguous observations leave room for multiple explanations; a plausible output alone cannot tell us which explanation is correct.

Takeaways

  1. The forward process buys tractability. Its Gaussian marginals let us construct arbitrary noise levels without simulating a training chain.
  2. Noise prediction learns a distribution-dependent quantity. The optimal predictor is a conditional expectation, equivalent to a rescaled noisy-data score—not perfect recovery of each injected noise realization.
  3. The objective is part of the contribution. The simplified loss changes timestep weighting; the ablation, not just the best FID, explains why that choice matters.
  4. A sample is more than a denoised estimate. Stochastic reverse transitions turn a shared network’s predictions into a generative trajectory, at substantial sequential cost.

DDPM is compelling because the mathematical and empirical stories meet: an analytically convenient corruption process becomes an effective image generator when paired with a carefully chosen learning problem. Understanding that meeting point is more useful than memorizing the sampling equation—and more transferable than treating every later diffusion capability as if it were already in this paper.
entry.summary: A visual review of DDPM: the tractable corruption process, the denoising objective, and what the experiments actually establish.

entry.title: a distill-style blog post
entry.content:
Equations

This theme supports rendering beautiful math in inline and display modes using MathJax 3 engine. You just need to surround your math expression with $$, like $$ E = mc^2 $$. If you leave it inside a paragraph, it will produce an inline expression, just like \(E = mc^2\).

In fact, you can also use a single dollar sign $ to create inline formulas, such as $ E = mc^2 $, which will render as $ E = mc^2 $. This approach provides the same effect during TeX-based compilation, but visually it appears slightly less bold compared to double-dollar signs $$, making it blend more naturally with surrounding text.

To use display mode, again surround your expression with $$ and place it as a separate paragraph. Here is an example:

\[\left( \sum_{k=1}^n a_k b_k \right)^2 \leq \left( \sum_{k=1}^n a_k^2 \right) \left( \sum_{k=1}^n b_k^2 \right)\]

Note that MathJax 3 is a major re-write of MathJax that brought a significant improvement to the loading and rendering speed.

Citations

Citations are then used in the article body with the <d-cite> tag. The key attribute is a reference to the id provided in the bibliography. The key attribute can take multiple ids, separated by commas.

The citation is presented inline like this: (a number that displays more information on hover). If you have an appendix, a bibliography is automatically created and populated in it.

Distill chose a numerical inline citation style to improve readability of citation dense articles and because many of the benefits of longer citations are obviated by displaying more information on hover. However, we consider it good style to mention author last names if you discuss something at length and it fits into the flow well — the authors are human and it’s nice for them to have the community associate them with their work.

Footnotes

Just wrap the text you would like to show up in a footnote in a <d-footnote> tag. The number of the footnote will be automatically generated.This will become a hoverable footnote.

Code Blocks

Syntax highlighting is provided within <d-code> tags. An example of inline code snippets: <d-code language="html">let x = 10;</d-code>. For larger blocks of code, add a block attribute:

var x = 25; function(x) { return x * x; }

Note: <d-code> blocks do not look good in the dark mode. You can instead use the standard Jekyll syntax highlight with the highlight liquid tag.

You can also write standard Markdown code blocks in triple ticks with a language tag, for instance:

def foo(x):
  return x

Interactive Plots

You can add interative plots using plotly + iframes :framed_picture:

The plot must be generated separately and saved into an HTML file. To generate the plot that you see above, you can use the following code snippet:

Details boxes

Details boxes are collapsible boxes which hide additional information from the user. They can be added with the details liquid tag:

Click here to know more

Additional details, where math \(2x - 1\) and code is rendered correctly.

Mermaid

This theme supports creating diagrams directly in markdown using Mermaid. Mermaid enables users to render flowcharts, sequence diagrams, class diagrams, Gantt charts, and more. Simply embed the diagram syntax within a mermaid code block.

To create a Gantt chart, you can use the following syntax:

```mermaid
gantt
    dateFormat  YYYY-MM-DD
    title A Gantt Diagram

    section Section
    Task A           :a1, 2025-01-01, 30d
    Task B           :after a1, 20d
    Task C           :2025-01-10, 12d
```

And here’s how it will be rendered:

gantt
    dateFormat  YYYY-MM-DD
    title A Gantt Diagram

    section Section
    Task A           :a1, 2025-01-01, 30d
    Task B           :after a1, 20d
    Task C           :2025-01-10, 12d

Similarly, you can also use it to create beautiful class diagrams:

```mermaid
classDiagram
direction LR
    class Animal {
        +String species
        +int age
        +makeSound()
    }
    class Dog {
        +String breed
        +bark()
    }
    class Cat {
        +String color
        +meow()
    }
    class Bird {
        +String wingSpan
        +fly()
    }
    class Owner {
        +String name
        +int age
        +adoptAnimal(Animal animal)
    }

    Animal <|-- Dog
    Animal <|-- Cat
    Animal <|-- Bird
    Owner "1" --> "0..*" Animal

    Dog : +fetch()
    Cat : +purr()
    Bird : +sing()
```

It will be presented as:

classDiagram
direction LR
    class Animal {
        +String species
        +int age
        +makeSound()
    }
    class Dog {
        +String breed
        +bark()
    }
    class Cat {
        +String color
        +meow()
    }
    class Bird {
        +String wingSpan
        +fly()
    }
    class Owner {
        +String name
        +int age
        +adoptAnimal(Animal animal)
    }

    Animal <|-- Dog
    Animal <|-- Cat
    Animal <|-- Bird
    Owner "1" --> "0..*" Animal

    Dog : +fetch()
    Cat : +purr()
    Bird : +sing()

With Mermaid, you can easily add clear and dynamic diagrams to enhance your blog content.

Diff2Html

This theme also supports integrating Diff2Html, a tool that beautifully renders code differences (diffs) directly in markdown. Diff2Html is ideal for showcasing code changes, allowing you to clearly present additions, deletions, and modifications. It’s perfect for code reviews, documentation, and tutorials where step-by-step code changes need to be highlighted—you can even introduce changes across multiple files at once.

```diff2html
diff --git a/utils/mathUtils.js b/utils/mathUtils.js
index 3b5f3d1..c7f9b2e 100644
--- a/utils/mathUtils.js
+++ b/utils/mathUtils.js
@@ -1,8 +1,12 @@
-// Basic math utilities
+// Extended math utilities with additional functions

-export function calculateArea(radius) {
-    const PI = 3.14159;
+export function calculateCircleMetrics(radius) {
+    const PI = Math.PI;
     const area = PI * radius ** 2;
+    const circumference = 2 * PI * radius;
+
+    if (!isValidRadius(radius)) throw new Error("Invalid radius");
+
     return { area, circumference };
 }

-export function validateRadius(radius) {
+export function isValidRadius(radius) {
     return typeof radius === 'number' && radius > 0;
 }

diff --git a/main.js b/main.js
index 5f6a9c3..b7d4e8f 100644
--- a/main.js
+++ b/main.js
@@ -2,9 +2,12 @@
 import { calculateCircleMetrics } from './utils/mathUtils';

-function displayCircleMetrics(radius) {
-    const { area } = calculateCircleMetrics(radius);
+function displayCircleMetrics(radius) {
+    const { area, circumference } = calculateCircleMetrics(radius);
     console.log(`Area: ${area}`);
+    console.log(`Circumference: ${circumference}`);
 }

-displayCircleMetrics(5);
+try {
+    displayCircleMetrics(5);
+} catch (error) {
+    console.error("Error:", error.message);
+}
```

Here’s how it will look when rendered with Diff2Html:

diff --git a/utils/mathUtils.js b/utils/mathUtils.js
index 3b5f3d1..c7f9b2e 100644
--- a/utils/mathUtils.js
+++ b/utils/mathUtils.js
@@ -1,8 +1,12 @@
-// Basic math utilities
+// Extended math utilities with additional functions

-export function calculateArea(radius) {
-    const PI = 3.14159;
+export function calculateCircleMetrics(radius) {
+    const PI = Math.PI;
     const area = PI * radius ** 2;
+    const circumference = 2 * PI * radius;
+
+    if (!isValidRadius(radius)) throw new Error("Invalid radius");
+
     return { area, circumference };
 }

-export function validateRadius(radius) {
+export function isValidRadius(radius) {
     return typeof radius === 'number' && radius > 0;
 }

diff --git a/main.js b/main.js
index 5f6a9c3..b7d4e8f 100644
--- a/main.js
+++ b/main.js
@@ -2,9 +2,12 @@
 import { calculateCircleMetrics } from './utils/mathUtils';

-function displayCircleMetrics(radius) {
-    const { area } = calculateCircleMetrics(radius);
+function displayCircleMetrics(radius) {
+    const { area, circumference } = calculateCircleMetrics(radius);
     console.log(`Area: ${area}`);
+    console.log(`Circumference: ${circumference}`);
 }

-displayCircleMetrics(5);
+try {
+    displayCircleMetrics(5);
+} catch (error) {
+    console.error("Error:", error.message);

Chartjs, Echarts and Vega-Lite

Chart.js is a versatile JavaScript library for creating responsive and interactive charts. Supporting multiple chart types like bar, line, pie, and radar, it’s an ideal tool for visualizing data directly in pngages.

Here’s an example of a JSON-style configuration that creates a bar chart in Chart.js:

```chartjs
{
  "type": "bar",
  "data": {
    "labels": ["2017", "2018", "2019", "2020", "2021"],
    "datasets": [
      {
        "label": "Population (millions)",
        "data": [12, 15, 13, 14, 16],
        "backgroundColor": "rgba(54, 162, 235, 0.6)",
        "borderColor": "rgba(54, 162, 235, 1)",
        "borderWidth": 1
      }
    ]
  },
  "options": {
    "scales": {
      "y": {
        "beginAtZero": true
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Vega-Lite is a declarative visualization grammar that allows users to create, share, and customize a wide range of interactive data visualizations. The following JSON configuration generates a straightforward bar chart:

```vega_lite
{
  "$schema": "https://vega.github.io/schema/vega/v5.json",
  "width": 400,
  "height": 200,
  "padding": 5,

  "data": [
    {
      "name": "table",
      "values": [
        {"category": "A", "value": 28},
        {"category": "B", "value": 55},
        {"category": "C", "value": 43},
        {"category": "D", "value": 91},
        {"category": "E", "value": 81},
        {"category": "F", "value": 53},
        {"category": "G", "value": 19},
        {"category": "H", "value": 87}
      ]
    }
  ],

  "scales": [
    {
      "name": "xscale",
      "type": "band",
      "domain": {"data": "table", "field": "category"},
      "range": "width",
      "padding": 0.1
    },
    {
      "name": "yscale",
      "type": "linear",
      "domain": {"data": "table", "field": "value"},
      "nice": true,
      "range": "height"
    }
  ],

  "axes": [
    {"orient": "bottom", "scale": "xscale"},
    {"orient": "left", "scale": "yscale"}
  ],

  "marks": [
    {
      "type": "rect",
      "from": {"data": "table"},
      "encode": {
        "enter": {
          "x": {"scale": "xscale", "field": "category"},
          "width": {"scale": "xscale", "band": 0.8},
          "y": {"scale": "yscale", "field": "value"},
          "y2": {"scale": "yscale", "value": 0},
          "fill": {"value": "steelblue"}
        },
        "update": {
          "fillOpacity": {"value": 1}
        },
        "hover": {
          "fill": {"value": "orange"}
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

TikZ

TikZ is a powerful LaTeX-based drawing tool powered by TikZJax. You can easily port TikZ drawings from papers, posters, and notes. For example, we can use the following code to illustrate Euler’s formula $ e^{i \theta} = \cos \theta + i \sin \theta $:

<script type="text/tikz">
  \begin{tikzpicture}
      \filldraw[fill=cyan!10, draw=blue, thick] (0,0) circle (2cm);

      \draw[->, thick] (-2.5,0) -- (2.5,0) node[right] {Re};
      \draw[->, thick] (0,-2.5) -- (0,2.5) node[above] {Im};

      \draw[->, thick, color=purple] (0,0) -- (1.5,1.5);
      \node[color=purple] at (1.1, 1.7) {$e^{i\theta}$};

      \draw[thick] (0.7,0) arc (0:45:0.7);
      \node at (0.9, 0.3) {$\theta$};

      \draw[dashed, color=gray] (1.5,1.5) -- (1.5,0) node[below, black] {$\cos \theta$};
      \draw[dashed, color=gray] (1.5,1.5) -- (0,1.5) node[left, black] {$\sin \theta$};
      \node at (2.2, 0) [below] {1};
      \node at (0, 2.2) [left] {$i$};
      \node at (1.5,1.5) [above right, color=blue] {$(\cos \theta \, \sin \theta)$};
  \end{tikzpicture}
</script>

Layouts

The main text column is referred to as the body. It is the assumed layout of any direct descendants of the d-article element.

.l-body

For images you want to display a little larger, try .l-page:

.l-page

All of these have an outset variant if you want to poke out from the body text a little bit. For instance:

.l-body-outset

.l-page-outset

Occasionally you’ll want to use the full browser width. For this, use .l-screen. You can also inset the element a little from the edge of the browser by using the inset variant.

.l-screen

.l-screen-inset

The final layout is for marginalia, asides, and footnotes. It does not interrupt the normal flow of .l-body sized text except on mobile screen sizes.

.l-gutter

Using the <aside> tag:

<aside><p>This is a sidenote using aside tag.</p></aside>
